lesson.grammar_point: softening disagreement (I see your point but, I am not sure that, tentative would and might, up to a point, with respect)

listenings.text: The conflict question is a trap for two kinds of candidates. The first kind has never had a conflict, or says so. Nobody believes that. The second kind tells me about a conflict he won, and describes the other person as an idiot. That candidate has just told me how he will talk about his classmates. What I want is a disagreement about something that mattered, with somebody you respected. I want to hear the words you actually used, because the words tell me whether you can disagree without making an enemy. And I want the ending, even if it was not a happy one. Sometimes the best answer is this one: we never agreed, but we found a way to work together anyway. That is exactly what a study group of forty executives from twelve countries will need from you.

The architect and I were at odds for most of the project. She wanted a glass facade on the west side of the building, and I knew the budget could not carry it. Our first two meetings got heated, and both times I stood my ground and won nothing. In the third meeting I changed one thing. I asked her to take me through the design from the beginning, and I did not interrupt her once. It took forty minutes. At the end I understood that the glass was not decoration. It was the only way to bring natural light into the patients’ rooms. So I stopped arguing about the facade and started arguing about the price. We found a supplier who could do it for twenty percent less, and she agreed to a simpler frame. Neither of us got what we wanted at the start. Both of us got something better.
